parsed_answer.content:
The design decision to place wait() and notify() (along with notifyAll()) directly inside the java.lang.Object class rather than the java.lang.Thread class often puzzles developers who are new to Java concurrency. To understand why this choice was made, we must look at how Java implements inter-thread communication, mutual exclusion, and monitor-based synchronization. In Java, every single object instantiated on the heap possesses an intrinsic lock, commonly known as a monitor. When a thread needs to coordinate access to a shared resource, it synchronizes on the monitor of the object that guards that resource. Because any object can serve as a synchronization monitor, the mechanism for putting a thread to sleep pending a state change (wait()) and waking it up when that state change occurs (notify()) must be universally available to all objects, not tied to the lifecycle of a specific thread.

If wait() and notify() were methods on the Thread class, it would create massive architectural limitations. A thread frequently needs to wait on conditions governed by multiple independent objects or shared data structures (such as a bounded buffer, a connection pool, or a queue). If synchronization primitives were bound to threads, a thread would not be able to wait on a specific monitor without coupling its identity to the resource. Furthermore, multiple threads often wait on the exact same resource monitor. Placing these methods in Object allows any thread holding that object's monitor to signal any other thread waiting on that exact same monitor, completely decoupling the waiter from the notifier. This design embodies the classical monitor pattern pioneered by C.A.R. Hoare and Per Brinch Hansen, where monitors are associated with shared data structures rather than the executing processes.

items: Every Java object header contains a Mark Word that stores synchronization state, including the identity of the thread currently owning the monitor, recursive lock counts, and pointers to the wait set.

When a thread invokes wait() on an object, it must already own that object's monitor (via a synchronized block or method). The JVM atomically releases the monitor and places the thread into the object's internal wait set, suspending its execution.

When another thread invokes notify() or notifyAll() on the same object, the JVM selects one or all threads from the object's wait set and moves them to the entry set, where they must re-contend for the monitor lock before resuming execution.

Because synchronization monitors are intrinsic to heap objects, the garbage collector and the JVM runtime manage monitor inflation and deflation seamlessly without exposing low-level thread scheduler handles.

parsed_answer.content: A classic production trap when using Object.wait() and notify() is failing to wrap the wait call in a while loop checking the condition. Because of spurious wakeups—where a thread wakes up from wait() without a call to notify() due to JVM implementation artifacts or OS signals—if you use an 'if' statement instead of a 'while' loop, your code will violate thread safety invariants. Always use 'while (!condition) { lock.wait(); }'.

title: Why are wait() and notify() in the Object class, not the Thread class?
